LESSON 7 OF 12·Injection, XSS & Client-Side Defenses

DOM-Based Vulnerabilities & Sanitization

Trace client-side sources and sinks in browser JavaScript, understand why innerHTML is dangerous, and sanitize rich HTML safely.

Beginner2 min
Why this matters

DOM-based vulnerabilities occur entirely inside browser JavaScript when code reads data from an untrusted client-side source (such as location.search, location.hash, or postMessage) and passes it into a dangerous DOM sink (such as element.innerHTML, document.write, or location.assign) without safe handling. Even if the server never sees the payload, the browser executes it in the application’s origin.

INTERACTIVE FLOW MODEL

Architecture & Trust Boundary Flow

Tracing how untrusted strings reach browser rendering sinks and how context-aware encoding neutralizes execution.

01 User Content
Safe text node
02 Template Renderer
Allowed
03 Browser DOM
  1. Source: User submits profile text, search query, or URL fragment.
  2. Boundary: Application places the value into a template or DOM text property.
  3. Sink: Browser renders readable text without creating new script elements.
01 Markup / Event Payload
Unencoded sink
02 Raw HTML Sink
Unblocked
03 Script Execution
  1. Source: Attacker supplies HTML tags, event attributes, or a javascript: URL.
  2. Boundary: Value is written raw via innerHTML or unescaped template interpolation.
  3. Sink: Browser parser executes injected script inside the victim's origin and session.
01 Untrusted Input
Encoded + restricted
02 Context Encoder + CSP
Verified
03 Inert DOM Text
  1. Source: Untrusted input arrives from the request, storage, or URL.
  2. Boundary: Output is encoded for the exact context (textContent / safe HTML sanitizer) and guarded by CSP.
  3. Sink: Browser displays literal characters; inline script execution is blocked.

What you'll learn

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • audit assignments to innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, document.write, eval, and Function
  • check window.addEventListener("message", ...) handlers for strict event.origin verification
  • review client-side redirects that read returnUrl or next parameters from the URL and pass them to location.href

How it works

  • A source is any browser property or API that an attacker can influence, including URL query strings, URL fragments, referrer headers, storage entries, or cross-window messages.
  • A sink is a browser DOM property or function that interprets strings as HTML markup, executable code, or navigation targets.
  • When JavaScript assigns untrusted text to innerHTML or outerHTML, the browser parses embedded tags and event handlers (such as <img src=x onerror=...>).
  • Using textContent or createElement assigns plain text nodes that the browser never parses as HTML markup.

The background

As single-page applications shifted rendering logic from server templates to client-side JavaScript in the 2010s, DOM-based XSS grew from a niche edge case into a primary web security focus.

Real-world examples

  • Client-side search widgets and tab routers frequently read location.hash or query parameters and inject them directly into a status banner via innerHTML.
  • Window postMessage listeners that fail to check event.origin can allow any third-party tab to send commands or markup into the page.

What to look for

  • Audit assignments to innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, document.write, eval, and Function.
  • Check window.addEventListener("message", ...) handlers for strict event.origin verification.
  • Review client-side redirects that read returnUrl or next parameters from the URL and pass them to location.href.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Use textContent, setAttribute, and DOM node creation APIs instead of innerHTML whenever rendering plain text.
  • When rich HTML or Markdown rendering is required, pass output through a vetted allowlist HTML sanitizer before inserting it into the DOM.
  • Validate redirect targets against same-origin paths before calling location.assign or location.replace.
  • Adopt browser Trusted Types where supported to block raw string assignments to dangerous DOM sinks.
